title: A clear work note
text: A useful work note is easy to understand. It identifies the task, gives the details that matter, and explains what should happen next. If someone else must act on the note, include a date or time where needed and check that names, amounts and instructions match the source. Before sharing a document, read it from beginning to end. Check spelling, punctuation, spacing and the order of information. Compare numbers with the original record one group at a time. If the source is unclear, ask the person responsible for it. Never invent a customer name, payment amount or delivery promise to make a document look complete.

title: Practice with care
text: Small habits add up over time. Sit comfortably, return your fingers to the home row, type at a steady pace and pause when your hands feel tense. Practise weak keys in short sets, then use them in real sentences. Keep a log that shows what you practised and what you will change next time. Save a clean copy of each exercise, and keep the original source unchanged so you can compare your work without guessing.

title: Check the details
text: A careful assistant checks names, dates, quantities and amounts before sharing a message. The first draft may be correct, but reading it again can reveal a missing space, an extra digit or a sentence that needs clarification. Work in small sections. Compare each section with its source, then review the whole document for meaning. If one detail cannot be confirmed, mark it for review and ask the person who owns the information.

title: A steady routine
text: A steady routine begins with a simple plan. Choose a short passage, set a timer, and type at a pace that feels controlled. When the timer ends, note the result and one area to improve. Take a short break, then practise a weak key in a few words. Do not turn every session into a race. Regular practice gives your hands time to learn useful movements and gives you evidence of progress.

title: Keep records useful
text: Good records make a team easier to support. Use clear headings, consistent dates and a file name that explains what the document contains. Keep fictional exercises separate from real work. When a list is long, check a small batch at a time and save before moving to the next task. A colleague should be able to understand the record without guessing what a column means. Clear work is easier to review, correct and hand over.
